claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed, non-uniform native oxide layer before exposure.
Controlled thermal oxidation at 300–400°C under controlled oxygen partial pressure can promote formation of a dense oxide film on Q235 steel.
The proposed treatment will make the native oxide layer thicker.
The proposed treatment will make the oxide layer more uniform.
The proposed treatment will produce an oxide layer predominantly composed of Fe2O3 rather than Fe3O4.
Fe3O4 is less protective than Fe2O3 in the proposed Q235 corrosion system.
A dense, thermally grown oxide film acts as a passive barrier on Q235 steel.
The thermally grown oxide film reduces transport of chloride ions and water to the steel substrate.
Reduced transport of aggressive species suppresses localized passive-layer breakdown.
Suppression of localized passive-layer breakdown delays initiation of pitting corrosion.
Thermally oxidized Q235 steel will have a slower corrosion rate than untreated Q235 steel under identical test environments.
Thermally oxidized Q235 steel will exhibit later pitting onset than untreated Q235 steel.
Thermally oxidized Q235 steel will exhibit less overall corrosion-related degradation than untreated Q235 steel.
The predicted protective effect will occur in salt-spray and immersion environments at both 25°C and 100°C.
The protective effect may be limited to corrosive challenges similar to the prescribed standardized salt-spray or immersion tests.
The long-term stability of the oxide film under cyclic or variable environmental conditions is undetermined.
Variability in the as-received oxide composition could influence the experimental outcome.
Minor steel impurities could alter thermal-oxidation kinetics and influence the outcome.
The study will compare thermally oxidized specimens with untreated Q235 controls under otherwise identical corrosion exposures.
Failure to obtain significantly lower corrosion rates, reduced pit density, or a markedly improved Fe2O3-rich uniform film will falsify the hypothesis.
